title: Booking gigs himself and never taking a 'no' personally
summary: He books his own gigs without management, treats a refusal as 'not right now', and relates his hesitation over the interview fee.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Are there issues in the business of music, as far as getting gigs and so forth, that are non- musical, generational, racial, man/woman, anything like that. Does that come into play as far as you know?

Well, I look at it like this. You get on the phone, you make a phone call to a club, you mention to the club owner, “I’d like to work your venue.” And either they’re available or they’re not. Now available to you or they’re not. Now I know a lot of people, musicians that I know, will tell you well you can’t do it on your own and you can’t call clubs because they don’t want to talk to musicians, and I have found that to be the absolute nontruth. The festivals that we just played, I booked them, I have a rider, I have a contract, I do all that kind of stuff. I found that I was not, at the time, viable enough to make management relevant for me. So I felt that I could do better by selling myself myself. And after you get over the initial shock of making the first phone call, which to this day I have never received a no. I have never called a club owner or head of a festival and received a no. Because I don’t look at it as a no. All it means is for this year there is no room. Then you call back the next year. There may be no room. And then the next year [finger snaps] you get the gig. So I never look at it as no, it just means not right now, which is that’s what it means. And so you never take it — the tough thing is to sell yourself and to have someone tell you no, and no take it personally. Because it’s not personal. The bottom line is are you viable enough to help this presenter, i.e. club owner, make the amount of money that you’re asking for so that it’s a win-win for him and you. So if it’s not then you have to bring him a product that will help him help you. That’s the way I look at it. So it’s the same as anybody in any other profession. And I think what happens with the musician, it’s tough. Because you have this artistic property where we practice all day and now I’ve got to sell myself and I’ve been practicing and I’ve got this

and I’ve got this to offer, and who is this guy to tell me that he doesn’t like me and my value is this and that. That’s when you make it personal. But the business aspect of it is, guess what, this is what it is. Case in point: you called my house. You said, “Javon, I’d like to have you come and speak to me about your life and your career.” And we spoke about the price. I said, “Oh man, I don’t know if I want to do that” and I hung up the phone. And when I hung up the phone I thought about and I said you know what? If I don’t sit down and give reflection of my career or sit down and articulate myself to someone, how is anyone going to know about me? So if I really want success I just walked the other way from success. So I called you back and I said, “You know what? I want the opportunity.” Because if it was good enough for Joe Williams, it’s good enough for Javon Jackson. But the musician is always weighing these situations where we feel we’re not being respected or we’re not getting what we deserve. And guess what? Nobody gets what they deserve. That’s why we negotiate. And some people don’t understand that. Negotiation means you don’t get what you want. If you got what you want there would be no negotiation.
